paper_title: Market-Conditioned JEPA: Learning from Unpredictable Market Shocks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Much of the variation in financial time series is driven by market-wide shocks that cannot be predicted from an asset's own history. Per-asset self-supervised learning treats this variation as irreducible noise. Under a latent factor model, we show that conditioning prediction on the realized market factor makes the asset's market exposure necessary for optimal prediction, while reducing the noise against which the asset-specific component is learned. Building on this insight, we introduce Market-Conditioned JEPA (MC-JEPA), a joint-embedding predictive architecture for financial time series. During training, we construct a leave-one-out market condition for each asset from the future target embeddings of other assets and incorporate it through factor loadings derived from the asset's own representation. On 11 years of minute-level Chinese A-share data, MC-JEPA improves over per-asset JEPA across nine targets spanning returns, market exposure, risk, and liquidity, with the strongest and most statistically significant gains in exposure, risk, and liquidity. It achieves the best RankIC on all liquidity targets and on return horizons from two hours to five days, outperforming time-series foundation models and self-supervised baselines, and delivers the best portfolio performance in a historical backtest. Ablations show that the return and exposure gains require the condition to be aligned with the realized market movement. After restoring the volatility scale removed by normalization, the predictor's factor loadings rank stocks by market beta nearly as well as a supervised probe, without labels. A synthetic factor-model study with known parameters shows that conditioning improves the recovery of both market exposure and the asset-specific component.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Portfolio construction and risk management require estimates of an assets return, volatility, liquidity, and market exposure, which measures how an asset responds to market-wide movements. Selfsupervised learning offers way to learn unified representation that supports these diverse tasks. Recent work has developed large number of time-series encoders and foundation models [Nie et al., 2023, Yue et al., 2022, Goswami et al., 2024, Das et al., 2024, Ansari et al., 2025], including models pretrained specifically on financial data [Shi et al., 2025]. However, these methods largely learn from individual time series, overlooking the common-factor structure of financial markets. Under this structure, much of an assets variation is driven by market-wide shocks [Sharpe, 1964, Fama and French, 1993], which are difficult to predict from an assets own history. Therefore, per-asset prediction objective treats the unpredictable component of these shocks as irreducible noise. This has two costs. First, the optimal predictor need only recover the assets conditional mean, without identifying how the asset responds to market movements. This provides limited supervision for market exposure. Second, the asset-specific signal that the predictor learns is observed against Code is available at https://github.com/OpenFinMind/MC-JEPA. Preprint. this market noise. Existing approaches that explicitly model cross-asset relationships [Xu et al., 2021, Li et al., 2024, Gu et al., 2021] are largely designed for supervised return prediction and often require cross-sectional information at inference. FactorVAE [Duan et al., 2022] is closely related to our approach, as it uses future cross-sectional returns to infer latent factors during training. However, it is supervised return prediction model built on engineered daily features, and its factor predictor still aggregates information across stocks at inference. In contrast, MC-JEPA learns selfsupervised representations by conditioning on market factor constructed from other assets future target embeddings. The resulting encoder operates independently on each asset at inference. Our key observation is that unpredictable market movements are observable during training through the realized futures of other assets. Conditioning prediction on these movements turns them from noise into supervision, shifting the learning objective from forecasting market shocks to capturing how each asset responds to them. We formalize this in latent factor model, showing that marketconditioned prediction makes exposure necessary for optimal prediction and removes the market component from the noise against which the asset-specific signal is learned. Building on this observation, we introduce Market-Conditioned JEPA (MC-JEPA), jointembedding predictive architecture [Assran et al., 2023] for financial time series. per-asset encoder embeds each assets recent history to representation, and predictor estimates its future target embeddings. During training, we construct leave-one-out market condition by aggregating the future target embeddings of other assets in the same panel. We then introduce factor-structured predictor that incorporates this condition through loadings derived from the assets own representation, following the structure of single-index factor model [Sharpe, 1964]. The market condition therefore cannot explain the target by itself. It helps only to the extent that the representation encodes the assets exposure. The market condition is privileged information [Duan et al., 2022] available only during training. At inference, the encoder is standard per-asset model that requires no cross-sectional information. We train MC-JEPA on minute-level candlesticks of the full cross-section of Chinese A-share stocks from 2015 to 2022 and evaluate the frozen representations with ridge probes on held-out 20232025 period. It improves on per-asset JEPA across nine targets spanning returns, market exposure, risk, and liquidity, with the largest and most significant improvements in exposure, risk, and liquidity. It achieves the highest RankIC on all liquidity targets and on returns from two hours to five days, outperforming time-series foundation models and self-supervised baselines. In historical trading backtest, it achieves the highest excess return and Sharpe ratio and the lowest maximum drawdown. Ablations show that the gains in return and exposure prediction depend on conditioning on the realized market movement over the same target period. Neither panel training alone nor conditioning on different date reproduces these gains. The factor loadings of the predictor are also interpretable. Rescaled by the price volatility that per-asset normalization removes, they rank stocks by market beta nearly as well as supervised probe, without any beta labels. synthetic factor-model study with known parameters further shows that conditioning improves the recovery of both the true market exposure and the asset-specific component. Our contributions are as follows: We show under latent factor model that market conditioning makes exposure necessary for optimal prediction and reduces noise in learning asset-specific signals. We introduce MC-JEPA, which uses market conditioning during training to learn standalone per-asset representations. We demonstrate improvements across financial prediction tasks and trading backtest, and show that the predictors factor loadings encode market exposure without labels.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Self-supervised learning for time series. Self-supervised learning for time series has three main directions. Contrastive methods learn representations by aligning augmented views or temporally related windows of series [van den Oord et al., 2019, Tonekaboni et al., 2021, Ennadir et al., 2025, Woo et al., 2022, Liu and Chen, 2024]. Masked-reconstruction methods recover hidden input patches from their surrounding context [Nie et al., 2023, Dong et al., 2023, Goswami et al., 2024]. More recently, large-scale pretraining has produced foundation models that forecast across diverse 2 Figure 1: MC-JEPA. During training, each assets future embedding is predicted both unconditionally and conditioned on market factor derived from the future target embeddings of other assets. The factor enters through loadings computed from the assets own representation. At inference, only the per-asset context encoder fθ is retained. time-series corpora [Das et al., 2024, Rasul et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2025, Ansari et al., 2025, He et al., 2025, HE et al., 2026], as well as general-purpose encoders that learn transferable representations [Lin et al., 2024, Fu and Hu, 2025]. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) [Assran et al., 2023] instead predict representations produced by slowly updated target encoder, avoiding the need to reconstruct unpredictable details in input space. JEPA objectives have been adapted to time series for control [Girgis et al., 2025], in-context forecasting [Verdenius et al., 2024], general representation learning [Ennadir et al., 2025] and anomaly prediction [He et al., 2026], and recently to equity modeling [Luo et al., 2026, Merchant et al., 2026]. Finance-specific foundation models such as Kronos [Shi et al., 2025] pretrain on large-scale candlestick data, yet recent evaluations find that both generic and finance-pretrained models give limited gains on financial returns [Rahimikia et al., 2025, Alonso and Franklin, 2026]. common limitation of these approaches is that they encode each asset independently and predict its future from its own history. However, in financial markets, much of an assets future variation is driven by market-wide shocks that cannot be inferred from its history alone. Consequently, such objectives provide little supervision for learning how an asset responds to these shocks. Our method addresses this limitation by retaining per-asset JEPA encoder while conditioning its predictor on market factor constructed from other assets future embeddings during training, which turns unpredictable market variation into learning signal for market exposure. Cross-asset dependencies in financial markets. Asset pricing has long modeled returns through asset-specific exposures to common factors, from the CAPM [Sharpe, 1964] to multi-factor models [Fama and French, 1993]. Such commonality extends beyond returns to order flow and liquidity [Hasbrouck and Seppi, 2001]. Two lines of work are particularly relevant to ours. First, factor-based neural models learn asset-specific exposures to shared factors. Conditional autoencoders [Gu et al., 2021] model exposures as nonlinear functions of asset characteristics and combine them with factors estimated from contemporaneous realized returns. FactorVAE [Duan et al., 2022] uses future cross-sectional returns as privileged information to infer latent factors during training. Both are supervised return-prediction models built on engineered daily features. In contrast, we bring the same factor exposure structure into self-supervised learning from raw time series. Asset-specific exposures are learned from each assets representation, and the market factor is constructed from other assets future target embeddings. Second, cross-asset neural models explicitly incorporate information from other assets through stock graphs and shared concepts [Xu et al., 2021], inter-stock attention with market gating [Li et al., 2024], spatiotemporal bootstrapping over correlated series [Wang et al., 2023], or correlation-aware adapters and group attention in foundation models [Cheng et al., 2026, Ansari et al., 2025]. These approaches generally rely on cross-sectional context at inference, while channel-mixing architectures can be less robust to distribution shift than channel-independent ones [Han et al., 2023]. Our method instead uses the market factor only to condition the predictor during training, leaving the deployed encoder fully per-asset and independent of cross-sectional inputs.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets and Baselines. We use 1-minute OHLCV bars of Chinese A-share stocks from 2015 to 2025. All splits are chronological. Pretraining uses decision times before July 2022. For evaluation we freeze each encoder and embed one window per stock and trading day, ending at the targets decision time. Daily targets are decided at the 15:00 close. Minute targets are decided at the 11:30 morning close. We fit ridge probes on 2019-01 to 2022-06, select the ridge penalty and the hyperparameters of MC-JEPA on 2022-07 to 2022-12, and report results on 2023-01 to 2025-12. We compare against three groups of baselines. (i) Finance-specific baselines. We use the Alpha158 daily factors [Yang et al., 2020]. Like the encoders, it is read out with ridge probe. (ii) Pretrained time-series foundation models. We use frozen Kronos [Shi et al., 2025], TimesFM-2.5 [Das et al., 2024], Chronos-2 [Ansari et al., 2025] and MOMENT [Goswami et al., 2024]. (iii) Self-supervised objectives. We compare objectives under the same encoder architecture, training data and compute budget. These include masked patch reconstruction (Masked recon.) [Nie et al., 2023, Dong et al., 2023], next-patch autoregression (Next-patch AR), TS2Vec [Yue et al., 2022], CPC [van den Oord et al., 2019], and per-asset JEPA (section 3.1). Ablations that isolate each component of our method are in section 4.3. Each encoder is read out from the [CLS] state if its objective trains it (JEPA variants and CPC), and from the mean of its patch states otherwise. For every baseline we checked that this is the better of the two readouts. Every encoder we train is run with three seeds, and we report the mean and standard deviation. Evaluation metrics. We evaluate nine downstream targets spanning returns, market exposure, risk, and liquidity. These include future returns over horizons from 120 minutes to 20 days, forward 20-day market beta, realized volatility, relative volume, and the fraction of next-day volume traded at the open. Our primary metric is RankIC, computed as the Spearman correlation between predictions and realized targets across stocks on each test day, averaged over the test period. We further assess economic value through historical long-only backtest using the Ret 20d predictions, reporting annualized excess return (AER), Sharpe ratio, information ratio (IR), and maximum drawdown (MDD). Appendix provides detailed definitions of all targets and metrics. Implementation details. Inputs are 1-minute OHLCV bars with context of = 960 bars, split into 96 patches of = 10 bars. The encoder is 12-layer Transformer with width = 256 (about 10M parameters). Targets are 30-bar blocks at horizons = {1, 60, 240} bars, spanning the next half hour to the next trading day. Each step samples 128 decision times, each with condition pool of Mt = 32 assets of which St = 8 are scored. The pool is drawn uniformly at random from all assets around t, and the scored assets are uniform random subset of the pool. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced MC-JEPA, self-supervised method that turns unpredictable market movements into supervision. Conditioning on the realized market factor makes market exposure necessary for optimal prediction and denoises the asset-specific signal. During training, factor-structured predictor conditions on leave-one-out market signal constructed from other assets future target embeddings, with loadings computed from the assets own representation. The condition is used only during training, leaving per-asset encoder that requires no cross-sectional information at inference. On 11 years of minute-level Chinese A-share data, MC-JEPA improves over per-asset JEPA on all nine targets spanning returns, market exposure, risk, and liquidity, most strongly on exposure, risk, and liquidity. It achieves the highest RankIC on all liquidity targets and on returns from two hours to five days, as well as the best performance in historical backtest. Ablations show that the gains in return and exposure prediction depend on aligning the market condition with the realized market movement over the target period. synthetic factor-model study further demonstrates that conditioning improves the recovery of both the true market exposure and the asset-specific component.

sections.title: 6 Limitations
sections.content: All real-data experiments are conducted on Chinese A-share equities at single bar frequency. Market-specific characteristics, including heavy retail participation, daily price limits, and T+1 settlement, may influence the impact of market-wide shocks on individual stocks. Whether our gains generalize to other markets, asset classes, or frequencies remains untested. Furthermore, Proposition 1 assumes linear factor model with access to the true factor, whereas MC-JEPA relies on an estimated leave-one-out market condition. Our use of single factor (K = 1) also leaves richer cross-sectional structure, such as industry and style factors, to be captured implicitly. Because inputs and targets are standardized per window, the learned loadings capture co-movement with the market rather than beta. Multiplying them by the windows price volatility recovers cross-sectional beta ranking. Targets that preserve each assets scale could make the loadings beta directly.

sections.content: Table 7 repeats the minute targets of Table 1 at shorter horizons, and Table 8 adds four daily targets. Appendix D.1 defines all of them. Probes, splits and seeds are the same as in Table 1. Minute horizons. The gains of MC-JEPA on the minute targets hold at every horizon. It is the best encoder on volume and second to CPC on volatility at 5, 30 and 60 minutes, as it is at 120 minutes. On returns it is best at 5 and 60 minutes, and at 30 minutes it trails per-asset JEPA within one seed standard deviation. Additional daily targets. The daily targets give more mixed picture. MC-JEPA is the best encoder on Volume 5d, consistent with Volume 1d. The daily risk targets favor CPC, which is the best encoder on all three and the best method on Vol 1d and Vol 5d. MC-JEPA ranks fourth among encoders on MDD 5d, behind CPC, next-patch AR and Chronos-2, and sixth on Vol 1d and Vol 5d, where Kronos-base and TimesFM-2.5 also lead it. Compared with per-asset JEPA, conditioning improves every daily target. Ablations. Tables 9 and 10 report the same targets for the variants of Table 3. Every variant with an aligned condition beats both per-asset and panel JEPA on all volatility, drawdown and volume targets, 17 at every horizon. The placebo stays below MC-JEPA on every target except Ret 60m, where the two tie. More factors help the risk and liquidity targets but hurt daily returns. Every risk and liquidity target is best at some > 1. The number of factors trades risk and liquidity prediction against return prediction. Pool size matters most at minute horizons. Vol 5m, Vol 30m and Vol 60m rise with Mt, as Vol 120m does, and Mt = 128 is above MC-JEPA on all three minute return horizons, although its Ret 30m varies widely across seeds. The daily targets change little with pool size. Hyperparameter selection. Table 11 reports the condition weight, factor-count and condition pool variants of Table 3 on the validation period, 2022-07 to 2022-12. We select λ and by Ret 1d and Ret 5d on this period. λ = 0.75 and = 1 are best on both. Larger improves Beta 20d and Vol 120m, and λ 0.75 matches or improves on smaller weights on every target except Ret 120m. Among pool sizes, Mt = 32 is best or tied on seven of the eight targets. Statistical significance. Table 12 tests whether the gains of MC-JEPA over per-asset JEPA and over the placebo condition are robust to day-to-day variation, and reports their consistency across seeds. For each target, we average the daily test RankIC of each method over its three seeds and compute the two-sided NeweyWest t-statistic of the mean daily difference. Overlapping labels make the daily RankIC autocorrelated, so target whose label spans trading days uses max(h, 6) lags, where 6 is the automatic choice 4(T /100)2/9 for 720 test days. This gives 20 lags for Ret 20d and Beta 20d and 6 for every other target. We also count the seeds for which the MC-JEPA run beats the run of the other method with the same seed. We report unadjusted tests at the 5% level. Against both methods, MC-JEPA is significantly better on every exposure, risk and liquidity target, with all three seed pairs in its favor. Return gains are smaller and less uniform. On daily returns, the gains over the placebo are significant on Ret 1d, Ret 5d and Ret 20d, and the gains over per-asset JEPA are significant on Ret 1d and Ret 20d but not on Ret 5d (t = 1.8), with all seed pairs in favor of MC-JEPA in each case.
